content:
There are many types of arthritis, but most fall into a few groups. Osteoarthritis is by far the most common and develops gradually. Inflammatory types, such as rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis and ankylosing spondylitis, are caused by the immune system. Crystal arthritis, such as gout, causes sudden severe attacks. Each type is treated differently, so getting the right diagnosis matters.

Osteoarthritis

The most common type. The cartilage lining the joint becomes thinner and the joint tries to repair itself, which can cause bony growths and changes in the joint. It most often affects knees, hips, hands and the spine, usually after 45.

Typical symptoms: pain with activity, short-lived stiffness after rest, sometimes swelling and grinding.

Treatment: exercise, weight management, pain relief, aids, and joint replacement for severe cases.

Inflammatory arthritis

The immune system attacks the joints, causing inflammation. Early treatment with disease-modifying medicines prevents damage.

  • Rheumatoid arthritis: usually affects small joints of hands and feet on both sides, with morning stiffness over 30 minutes and fatigue.
  • Psoriatic arthritis: occurs with psoriasis. It can cause swollen "sausage" fingers or toes, heel pain and nail changes.
  • Ankylosing spondylitis (axial spondyloarthritis): mainly affects the spine and pelvis, with back pain that is worse at rest and better with movement, starting before 45.
  • Enteropathic arthritis: linked with Crohn's disease or ulcerative colitis.
  • Reactive arthritis: develops after an infection, often a bowel or sexually transmitted infection, and usually settles within months.
  • Juvenile idiopathic arthritis: arthritis that starts before the age of 16.

Crystal arthritis

  • Gout: uric acid crystals form in a joint, causing sudden severe pain, redness and swelling, often in the big toe. Treatment includes medicines for attacks and medicines to lower uric acid long-term.
  • Pseudogout (CPPD): calcium crystals cause similar sudden attacks, often in the knee or wrist, mainly in older people.

Connective tissue diseases

These autoimmune conditions can affect joints and other parts of the body:

  • Lupus (SLE): joint pain, rashes, fatigue and sometimes kidney or blood problems
  • Sjögren's syndrome: dry eyes and mouth with joint pain
  • Systemic sclerosis (scleroderma): skin thickening, cold fingers and joint pain

Conditions that affect muscles and soft tissues

  • Polymyalgia rheumatica: stiffness and pain in shoulders and hips, mainly in over 50s, treated with steroids
  • Fibromyalgia: widespread pain and fatigue. It is not a type of arthritis but often affects people who have arthritis.

Infection in a joint

Septic arthritis is an infection inside a joint. It causes a hot, swollen, very painful joint, often with fever, and is a medical emergency.

How doctors tell them apart

Your GP will ask about which joints hurt, how long stiffness lasts, any swelling and other symptoms such as rashes or bowel problems. Blood tests, X-rays, ultrasound or joint fluid tests may help. Osteoarthritis can usually be diagnosed from symptoms alone. Suspected inflammatory arthritis should be referred to a rheumatologist.

Why the type matters

Treatments differ. Exercise helps all types, but inflammatory arthritis also needs medicines that calm the immune system, while gout needs medicines that lower uric acid. If your arthritis is not improving as expected, ask whether the diagnosis should be reviewed.

Living with arthritis

Whatever the type, staying active, keeping to a healthy weight, pacing and getting support with work, mood and daily tasks all make a difference.

Questions to ask your GP

  • What type of arthritis do you think I have, and why?
  • Do I need blood tests, an X-ray or a referral?
  • What treatment and exercise do you recommend for my type?
  • What should I do if my symptoms change?

It can help to bring a list of the joints affected, how long stiffness lasts and any other symptoms, such as rashes or eye problems. Photos of swollen joints are also useful if the swelling comes and goes.

When to get urgent help

Call 999 or go to A&E if you have:

  • a joint that suddenly becomes hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially if you feel feverish or unwell (this can be a joint infection)
  • chest pain, sudden breathlessness, or signs of a stroke such as face drooping, arm weakness or slurred speech

Contact NHS 111 or your GP the same day if symptoms are getting worse quickly, you cannot put weight on a leg, or you are worried and not sure where to go. If you are under a rheumatology team, use their advice line for flares and medicine questions.
